toc.title: Can you come out of shutdown?
Co-regulation, if you can access it

blocks.p: Have you ever felt so overwhelmed that you just shut down, emotionally and physically? Maybe you've had a sudden loss of energy, or a chronic feeling of numbness or disconnection from the world around you. These are common signs of what's known as a dorsal vagal shutdown. It's a physiological reaction to stress that can leave us feeling helpless and unable to cope.

You might think something's wrong with you, or that things won't improve. You might be feeling hopeless or helpless. So let's look at what a dorsal vagal shutdown actually is, how to recognize it, and some concrete next steps toward a life with a bit more connection and a bit more hope.
Dorsal vagal shutdown is a potential physiological response to stress. It happens when our body cannot run away and cannot fight back, and so it collapses.

It's a limp collapse. That's the difference from freeze, which is more of a tense stiffening. They're both immobile, but a dorsal vagal shutdown is that limp collapse. It kicks in due to a life threat: our body detects that not just its safety is in danger, but that its life is under threat.

That's how it evolved within us. It's intended to help us survive a life threat. In the shutdown state, the body's functions slow down significantly, and that makes us appear dead. We look like a corpse. Heart rate goes down, breathing slows down a lot, digestion is inhibited, and the body might feel numb or disconnected. Dissociation might happen.

So if a predator sees this, which looks like death, it's more likely to mosey on by. And if it's in its own fight energy, that predatory hunting energy, it probably isn't going to stop. It needs to use up its own energy, so it goes right past the prey that's in shutdown and chases down the prey that's running away. That's the evolutionary intent of shutdown: to mimic death.

A bunch of things can cause a dorsal vagal shutdown. It could be a physically traumatic incident, something you went through physically. It could be something emotionally traumatic. It could be chronic stress, or a chronic illness. All of these can trigger, or help to trigger, a shutdown, especially as they add up on each other.

Chronic stress could be financial problems, relationship issues, or work-related stress. Any one of those might not be enough to put someone into shutdown. But if you have those going on chronically, plus a chronic illness, plus a specific, more acute traumatic incident, plus a childhood with poor attachment, then the more these add up, the more they can lead to a flavor of shutdown in your system.

Chronically existing in shutdown isn't the same as the immediate, life threat kind of shutdown. What I described above is prey surviving in the wild. As human beings, we have more of a chronic existence in shutdown, and that looks different.

Shutdown can look obvious from the outside, especially in a life threat situation. You'll see someone collapse and go limp. If you look on YouTube, you can find videos of people passing out on roller coasters. That's a dorsal vagal shutdown. They can't run away, they can't fight, and their body collapses.

For someone in that ongoing, chronic stress, it can be much harder to tell that they're in a dominant dorsal vagal shutdown. What they're going through might include numbness or even dissociation. They might feel disconnected from reality or from other people. They might have low energy and fatigue.

My therapy clients describe something really similar when I ask them what it's like to be in shutdown, or to be depressed. They tell me it feels like they're in a dark room and they're all alone. Usually they give an image of lying on the ground, not in a tense fetal position, but limp and collapsed. Sometimes the room has walls, sometimes it doesn't. But they always say they're alone, and they always say it's dark. The emotions are often hopeless, helpless, sad, or numb. That's what they consistently describe.

Can you see that from the outside looking in? No, of course not. Someone in shutdown, especially in a school system, doesn't cause problems. Their motivation might be super low, but they're not the loud kid in class. They're not the person at Starbucks throwing a fit because their coffee was wrong. The person in shutdown pretty much goes along. They don't want attention. Not that they choose it, but biologically they have an impulse to hide, and that permeates their day-to-day life.
Trauma is not the thing you went through. It's the impact of the thing you went through, or the impact of the things you didn't get.

The thing you went through could be an attack, an assault, or an accident. Something you went through may have left you in a traumatized state. Likewise, you're supposed to get healthy, safe attachment with caregivers growing up. If you didn't get that, that could leave you in a traumatized state too. Some events, or some absences, are obviously more potentially traumatic than others. But the point is that trauma is the impact.

And the impact is being stuck in a defensive state: flight, fight, shutdown, or maybe freeze. Whatever the path, what these have in common is difficulty or inability to access the safety state. Trauma is being stuck in defense and having a really hard time accessing, or holding on to, safety.
So how does shutdown fit in? There are two paths.

Not getting what you needed. This path relates to the impulse to attach to others. Children are biologically predisposed to attach to safe others. They must. When that impulse can't be fulfilled, their safety state can't develop. That often leaves them in more of a shutdown state, especially if they don't have any attachment at all.

Going through something. This path can result in freeze. Freeze is a combination of shutdown's immobility plus sympathetic flight and fight. The body is prepared to run away or fight, but it can't, either by force or through perception. Either way, that flight and fight energy gets locked into the system, and what locks it in is the immobility of shutdown. So the freeze path of trauma directly involves shutdown, but it's not alone. It's with flight and fight.

That frozen flight and fight energy might explode in a rage, erupt into a panic attack, be felt as overwhelm, or pop up during flashbacks or nightmares. It gets triggered by contexts similar to whatever that person went through. Freeze and shutdown are different, but they both involve immobilization.

blocks.h: Can you come out of shutdown?

blocks.p: I think it's very much possible to come out of a chronic dorsal vagal shutdown. Our autonomic nervous system evolved to do it. We come out of shutdown, out of immobility and collapse, up into flight and fight. The sympathetic system kicks on and energy comes back into the system. And if we can successfully run away or use aggression, we can get to safety and access our safety state again.

I think wild animals do just fine with that. Human beings are something different. There are a whole bunch of reasons we stay stuck, things we do to ourselves and things we do to each other, but that's a whole other conversation.

So for us, it's not quick. We can come out of shutdown, but we have to emerge slowly. As we slowly emerge, more and more flight and fight energy comes back into the system. That's what we want. It's a good thing, as long as we can welcome it and tolerate it a bit at a time.

That returning energy can be overwhelming. It can be scary, especially if you're not prepared for it and don't know what to expect. That's often what stops the process of self-regulation and trauma recovery, which is sad.

So we turn to behavioral adaptations: overeating, binge-watching something, mindlessly swiping through our phone, drug use, or a whole bunch of other things. We do these to cope with, ignore, minimize, or not deal with what's inside us, that natural self-regulation process.

Eventually we have to move beyond these behavioral adaptations, and even beyond the ways we typically cope or manage. Eventually we have to mindfully embrace the experience of being in shutdown, and also the experience of flight and fight energy coming back into the system, as part of the natural process of climbing the [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system). I don't think a dorsal vagal shutdown needs to be permanent. I think it's generally possible to live a more connected, more fulfilling life. It is a long process.

blocks.h: Co-regulation, if you can access it

blocks.p: One thing that can help, if you can access it, is co-regulation. When Deb Dana was on the podcast a long time ago, she gave this really great analogy:

q: To get a turtle to come out of the shell, you don't knock on its shell and you don't shake them... You just kinda sit there patiently... But you really have to be beaming that ventral vagal energy to that system.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: What she's saying is that coming out of shutdown can't be forced. You can't yell at somebody enough to get them out of shutdown. You can't shake them out of it.

First, they have to detect that it's safe to come out. They have to know it's safe. I don't mean knowing on a cognitive level, although maybe that's part of it. I mean knowing biologically: neurocepting cues of safety from the environment, whether that's the literal physical environment or the people and relationships in it. When we get cues of safety from a safe other person, that's co-regulation. That's what Deb Dana means by beaming safety cues. So if someone in shutdown can connect with safe others who give them a sense of safety, that could be helpful.

But I know this can be difficult for someone in shutdown, because they tend to want to be alone, or tend to be alone. Connection is quite a challenge for them. It can absolutely help, but it might not be where you start.
The starting point might be your external environment. That's where I recommend people start: with the safety cues around them.

Everything around you right now, you're neurocepting as safe, dangerous, or maybe neutral. Everything around you is affecting your polyvagal state: the lighting, the sound, the smells, the proximity of things. All of it affects your potential to neurocept safety, to come out of shutdown or whatever defensive state you're in, and to climb your polyvagal ladder.
Here's how to work with that:

ol: Assess your space. Do a quick assessment of your home. Where do you feel safest? What cues do you have where you feel more safety in your system, more calm, where you can breathe easier? And notice what takes you away from safety.

Set up passive safety cues. It's possible to change your environment to give yourself more safety cues. Passive cues are things you don't have to consciously notice. They simply provide a steady stream of safety: music, or silence, or the lighting, whatever it is for you. When we're in shutdown, the environment is usually overstimulating or overwhelming, so this is your opportunity to take control and give yourself less stimulation, if that feels right for you. Ask yourself how you feel, and when you tweak things, how does that feel?

Mindfully experience them. Then be a little more active about those safety cues. If you set up dim lighting in your room and feel more safety in that, don't just set it up and then swipe on your phone. Don't set it up and go on TikTok. (I'd recommend not going on TikTok at all, but you get the idea.) Set up the lighting or the scent or the music, then sit, or lie down, it doesn't matter, and experience the safety from the environment.

Allow the immobility. I know it sounds scary, but in shutdown your body has an impulse to immobilize. So allow yourself to be immobile without judgment. Be in your shutdown immobility with curiosity, and be curious about what it's like to be immobile in your safety environment.

Let the energy return, little by little. If you can allow mindful experiencing of your shutdown state in your safety environment, your natural capacity for self-regulation might start to emerge. As you come out of shutdown, flight and fight energy might start to fill your system. Ideally, we want that to happen little by little by little.

blocks.p: If you're experiencing significant or debilitating symptoms of dorsal vagal shutdown, seek professional help. In my opinion, working with someone who's polyvagal informed can be extremely helpful.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: I do believe there's a lot of hope in coming out of shutdown. Shutdown has been my dominant state, my home away from home. I've spent a lot of time in shutdown in my life. So I know coming out of it is possible.

It's a slow process. You do it little by little. You invite your sympathetic flight and fight energy in little by little, and you feel it little by little, without judgment, with curiosity, and from your safety state.
